''''' Artemisia tridentata''''', commonly called '''big sagebrush''',<ref name="MDW">MacKay, Pam (2013), ''Mojave Desert Wildflowers'', 2nd ed., {{ISBN|978-0762780334}}, p. 264.</ref> '''Great Basin sagebrush'''<ref name=MDW/> or simply '''sagebrush''' (one of [[Sagebrush|several related species]] of this name), is an aromatic [[shrub]] from the family [[Asteraceae]].

It grows in arid and semi-arid conditions, throughout a range of cold [[desert]], [[steppe]], and [[mountain]] habitats in the [[Intermountain West]] of [[North America]]. Big sagebrush and other ''Artemisia'' shrubs are the [[Dominance (ecology)|dominant]] plant species across large portions of the [[Great Basin]].

Sagebrush provides food and [[habitat]] for a variety of species, such as [[sage-grouse]], [[pronghorn]], [[gray vireo]], [[pygmy rabbit]], and [[mule deer]]. Several major threats exist to sagebrush ecosystems, including human settlements, conversion to [[agricultural]] land, [[invasive plant species]], and [[wildfire]]s.

[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] have used the plant medicinally. It is also useful as firewood.

==Description==
Big sagebrush is a coarse, many-branched, pale-grey shrub with yellow [[flower]]s and silvery-grey [[foliage]], which is generally {{Convert|0.5–3|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall.<ref>{{cite book|author=Brayshaw, T.C.|chapter=Artemisia tridenta Nutall. (Big Sagebrush)|title=Trees and Shrubs of British Columbia|publisher=University of British Columbia Press|year=1996|isbn=9780774805643|page=337|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2pzdJ8eddAEC&pg=PA337}}</ref> A deep [[taproot]] {{Convert|1–4|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in length, coupled with laterally spreading roots near the surface, allows sagebrush to gather water from both surface precipitation and the water table several meters beneath. Big sagebrush that is over a meter tall is an indicator of arable land, because it prefers deep, basic soils.<ref name="Mozingo-1987-p271">{{cite book|author=Mozingo, Hugh N.|title=Shrubs Of The Great Basin: A Natural History|publisher=University of Nevada Press|year=1987|isbn=9780874171129|page=271|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ziSx1F854OUC&pg=PA271}}</ref> Sagebrush is generally long-lived once it makes it past the seedling stage, and can reach ages of over 100 years.<ref name="Barbour-2000-p259">{{cite book |author=Barbour, Michael G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ra2QzAh9xdIC&pg=PA259 |title=North American Terrestrial Vegetation |author2=Billings, William D. |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2000 |isbn=9780521559867 |page=259}}</ref>

[[File:Artemisia tridentata 2.jpg|thumb|left|Leaves and flowers]]

The species has a strong pungent fragrance (especially when wet) due to the presence of [[camphor]], [[terpenoid]]s and other [[volatile oils]].<ref name=shakhnoza>{{cite book|author=Shakhnoza, Azimova S.|title=Lipids, Lipophilic Components and Essential Oils from Plant Sources|publisher=Springer|year=2012|isbn=9780857293237|page=844|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w74gD4-YxaQC&pg=PT844|display-authors=etal}}</ref> The taste is bitter and, together with the odor, serves to discourage browsing by many herbivores. It is an [[evergreen]] shrub, keeping some of its leaves year-round (although it loses many of them in the late summer).<ref>{{cite book|author=Baldwin, Bruce G.|title=The Jepson Desert Manual: Vascular Plants of Southeastern California|publisher=University of California Press|year=2002|isbn=9780520227750|page=117|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SRU8v_1glgsC&pg=PA117}}</ref> The [[leaves]]—attached to the branches at the [[Glossary of botanical terms#axillary|axillary nodes]]—are wedge-shaped, {{Convert|1–3|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long and 0.3–1 cm broad, with the wider outer tips divided into three lobes (hence the scientific name ''tridentata'').<ref>{{cite book|author=Ferris, Roxana A. |author2=Abrams, LeRoy|chapter=Artemisia tridentata Nutt. Sagebrush|title=Illustrated Flora of the Pacific States, Vol. IV: Bignonias to Sunflowers|publisher=Stanford University Press|year=1960|isbn=9780804700061|page=412|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y9akJhAEJc8C&pg=PA412}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|author1=Stuart, John D.  |author2=Sawyer, John O. |name-list-style=amp|chapter=Big Sagebrush (''Artemisia tridentata'')|title=Trees and Shrubs of California|publisher=University of California Press|year=2001|isbn=9780520221093|page=169|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=me9WDy7GXioC&pg=PA169}}</ref><ref name="Clarke-1978-p134">{{Cite book |author=Clarke, Charlotte B. |title=Edible and Useful Plants of California |publisher=University of California Press |year=1978 |isbn=9780520032675 |page=134 |chapter=Big Sagebrush |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fzckXaQgsDEC&pg=PA134}}</ref> The leaves are covered with fine silvery hairs.<ref name="Kershaw-2001-p25">{{Cite book |author=Kershaw, Linda |url=https://archive.org/details/rarevascularplan00kers |title=Rare Vascular Plants of Alberta |publisher=University of Alberta |year=2001 |isbn=9780888643193 |page=[https://archive.org/details/rarevascularplan00kers/page/25 25] |chapter=Big sagebrush |url-access=registration}}</ref>

The plant flowers in the late summer or early fall.<ref>{{cite book|author=Raven, Peter H.|title=Native Shrubs of Southern California|publisher=University of California Press|year=1996|isbn=9780520010505|page=54|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PGDlRiWs7JQC&pg=PA54}}</ref> The small yellow flowers are in long, loosely arranged tubular clusters.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tilford, Gregory L.|title=Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West|publisher=Mountain Press Publishing|year=1997|isbn=9780878423590|page=208|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P_s7sD11RM8C&pg=PT16}}</ref> The fruits are seed-like and have a small amount of hairs on the surface.<ref name="Kershaw-2001-p25" />

Big sagebrush can also [[Vegetative reproduction|reproduce through sprouts]], which shoot up from the underground rhizome. The sprouts are an extension of the parental plant while seedlings are completely individualistic to any other plant. Among these two strategies, the seedlings need more moisture for germination and early survival. This is due to the sprouts being connected to already healthy and associated plants while the new seedlings will start anew.{{citation needed|date=July 2012}}

=== Chemistry ===
Sagebrush essential oil contains approximately 40% ''l''-camphor; 20% [[pinene]]; 7% [[cineole]]; 5% [[methacrolein]]; and 12% [[Terpinene|''a''-terpinene]], ''d''-camphor, and [[sesqiterpenoids]].<ref name="shakhnoza" />

== Taxonomy ==
Much discussion and disagreement revolves around the question of how to divide the species into varieties and subgenera. The following [[subspecies]] are accepted by some authors, though others advocate different systems.<ref name="Barbour-2000-p259" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_artrw8.pdf |access-date=16 March 2022 |website=Plants.usda.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Artemisia tridentata in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250066171 |access-date=16 March 2022 |website=Efloras.org}}</ref>
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''tridentata''''' ("basin big sagebrush")
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''vaseyana''''' ("mountain big sagebrush")
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''wyomingensis''''' ("Wyoming big sagebrush") – Found in the drier portions of the [[sagebrush steppe]]. Shrub density is generally less than 1 plant/m<sup>2</sup>, with little herbaceous cover surrounding the shrub.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Barbour, Michael G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YNAWPSMm2CUC&pg=PA599 |title=Terrestrial Vegetation of California |publisher=University of California Press |year=2007 |isbn=9780520249554 |page=599 |display-authors=etal}}</ref>
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''xericensis''''' ("scabland big sagebrush")
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''spiciformis''''' ("subalpine big sagebrush")
* '''''A. tridentata'' subsp. ''parishii''''' ("Parish's big sagebrush")
[[File:sagebrush.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.36|[[Eastern Washington]]]]

==Distribution and habitat==
''Artemisia tridentata'' grows in arid and semi-arid conditions, throughout the [[Intermountain West]] of [[North America]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Smith, Stanley D.|title=Physiological Ecology of North American Desert Plants|publisher=Springer|year=1997|isbn=9783540531135|page=107|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JLHgAxaDpIAC&pg=PA107|display-authors=etal}}</ref> Sagebrush is not a [[desert]] plant, but rather a resident of the [[steppe]], in areas that receive {{convert|18|–|40|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} of annual precipitation.<ref>{{cite book|author=Mozingo, Hugh N.|title=Shrubs Of The Great Basin: A Natural History|publisher=University of Nevada Press|year=1987|isbn=9780874171129|page=270|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ziSx1F854OUC&pg=PA270}}</ref> Big sagebrush and other ''[[Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]'' species are the dominant plants across large portions of the [[Great Basin]], covering some {{convert|422000|sqmi|km2|abbr=off}} in 11 western U.S. states and Canadian provinces.<ref>{{cite book|author=Müller-Schwarze, Dietland|title=Chemical Ecology of Vertebrates|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2006|isbn=9780521363778|page=310|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HaaFlUw4goIC&pg=PA310}}</ref> The range extends northward through [[British Columbia]]'s southern interior, south into [[Baja California]], and east into the western [[Great Plains]] of [[New Mexico]], [[Colorado]], [[Nebraska]], and the [[Dakotas]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map |url=http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Artemisia%20tridentata.png |access-date=16 March 2022 |website=Bonap.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Artemisia tridentata Calflora |url=https://www.calflora.org/app/taxon?crn=725 |access-date=16 March 2022 |website=Calflora.org}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:SageGrouse21.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.79|[[Sage grouse]]]]
Sagebrush provides food and [[habitat]] for a variety of animal species, such as [[sage grouse]], [[pronghorn]], [[gray vireo]], [[pygmy rabbit]], and [[mule deer]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=Smith, Genny|title=Sierra East: Edge of the Great Basin|publisher=University of California Press|year=2000|isbn=9780520086890|page=168|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PEsRggHM9LUC&pg=PA168}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|author=Barbour, Michael G.|title=Terrestrial Vegetation of California|publisher=University of California Press|year=2007|isbn=9780520249554|page=593|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YNAWPSMm2CUC&pg=PA593|display-authors=etal}}</ref> It is especially important to game animals during the winter.<ref name="Knopf">{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/400 |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0394731271 |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/400 400]}}</ref> Sagebrush also creates habitat for many species of [[grass]]es and [[herb]]s. Besides providing shade and shelter from the wind, the long taproot of sagebrush draws water up from deep in the soil, some of which becomes available to these surrounding [[shallow-rooted]] plants.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Cresser, Malcolm S.  |author2=Smith, Keith A. |name-list-style=amp|title=Soil and Environmental Analysis: Modern Instrumental Techniques|publisher=CRC Press|year=2003|isbn=9780824756949|page=364|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2oZRTlbTuh8C&pg=PA364}}</ref>

The terpenoid compounds in big sagebrush are thought to ward off herbivores. These oils, at high concentrations, are toxic to the [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] [[bacteria]] in the [[rumen]] of some [[ruminant]]s like deer and cattle.<ref>Nagy, JG and RP Tengerdy. 1968. Antibacterial action of essential oils of Artemisia as an ecological factor: II. Antibacterial action of the volatile oils of Artemisia tridentata (big sagebrush) on bacteria from the rumen of mule deer" ''Applied and Environmental Microbiology'' 16(3) 441–44.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|author=Rogosic, J.|chapter=Importance of plants with medicinal properties in herbivore diets|editor=Casasús, I. |editor2=Rosati, Andrea|title=Animal Farming and Environmental Interactions in the Mediterranean Region|publisher=Wageningen Academic Pub.|year=2011|isbn=9789086861842|pages=47–48|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2wRCo3uNlVgC&pg=PA47|display-authors=etal}}</ref> Pronghorn are the only large [[herbivore]] to browse sagebrush extensively.<ref>{{cite book|author=Lentz, David L.|title=Imperfect Balance: Landscape Transformations in the Precolumbian Americas|publisher=Columbia University Press|year=2000|isbn=9780231111560|page=49|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LXw6aaHYpjMC&pg=PA49}}</ref> Damage to sagebrush plants caused by grazing herbivores results in the release of volatile chemicals, which are used to signal a warning to nearby plants, so that they can increase the production of repellent chemical compounds. This plant-to-plant communication can take place at distances of up to {{Convert|60|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}}.<ref>{{cite book|author=Holopainen, Jarmo K. |author2=Blande, James D.|chapter=Molecular Plant Volatile Communication|editor=López-Larrea, Carlos|title=Sensing in Nature|publisher=Springer|year=2012|isbn=9781461417033|page=20|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f3TNR_Inv5oC&pg=PA20}}</ref>
[[File:Antilocapra americana.jpg|thumb|right|[[Pronghorn]] are the only large herbivores who browse on sagebrush extensively.]]
Several major threats exist to sage brush ecosystems, including human settlements, conversion to [[agricultural]] land, [[invasive plant species]], [[wildfire]]s, and [[climate change]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Knick, Steven T. |author2=Connelly, John|title=Greater Sage-Grouse: Ecology and Conservation of a Landscape Species and Its Habitats|publisher=University of California Press|year=2011|isbn=9780520267114|page=145|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c8ubKrmXwK8C&pg=PA145}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Shepherd, Jay F. |display-authors=etal |chapter=Landscape Fragmentation and Non-Breeding Greater Sage-Grouse|title=Ecology, Conservation, and Management of Grouse|date=4 September 2011 |editor=Sandercock, Brett K.|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=9780520270060|page=78|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vuocreLnCp4C&pg=PA78|display-editors=etal}}</ref>  Due to large periods of time where sagebrush was the primary shrub, many species have become adapted to this habitat. The burning of the shrubs leads to habitat loss of many species and can be very detrimental to the ecosystem as a whole.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wambolt|first=C.L.|author2=Walhof, Frisina|title=Recovery of big sagebrush communities after burning in south-western Montana|journal=Journal of Environmental Management|date=March 2001|volume=61|issue=3|pages=243–252|doi=10.1006/jema.2000.0411|pmid=11381951 |bibcode=2001JEnvM..61..243W }}</ref> Furthermore, the destruction of native grasses and forbs by grazing and fire creates conditions where invasive plants colonize the area. The invasive species which has destroyed the largest amount of sagebrush habitat is [[Downy brome|cheatgrass]] (''Bromus tectorum''). Since its accidental introduction in the 1890s,<ref>{{cite book|author=Radosevich, Steven R.|title=Weed Ecology: Implications for Management|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=1997|isbn=9780471116066|pages=29–30|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XA1ioKqctwwC&pg=PA29|display-authors=etal}}</ref> cheatgrass has radically altered the native shrub ecosystem by replacing indigenous vegetation,<ref name="Radosevich-2007-p26">{{cite book|author=Radosevich, Steven R.|title=Ecology of Weeds and Invasive Plants: Relationship to Agriculture and Natural Resource Management|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2007|isbn=9780471767794|pages=26–29|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2paeqsOV2I8C&pg=PA26|display-authors=etal}}</ref> and by creating a fire cycle that is too frequent to allow sagebrush to re-establish itself. Sagebrush lacks [[fire tolerance]] and relies on wind-blown seeds from outside the burned area for re-establishment.<ref>This is in contrast to many of the other plants which share its habitat, such as [[Rabbitbrush]], [[Ephedra (genus)|Ephedra]] and bunchgrasses, which can root-sprout after a fire.</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Boersma, P.D. |author2=Van Buren, Amy N.|title=Invasive Species in the Pacific Northwest|publisher=University of Washington Press|year=2006|isbn=9780295985961|page=36|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NfsVwjG_TAMC&pg=PA36}}</ref> Some tree species have also encroached on big sagebrush habitat. For example, in the late 20th century, ''[[Abies concolor]]'' (white fir) was out-competing big sagebrush in [[Warner Mountains]] in California.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Vale|first=Thomas|title=Invasion of big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) by white fir (Abies concolor) on the southeastern slopes of the Warner Mountains, California|journal=Western North American Naturalist|year=1975|volume=35|issue=3}}</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Cahuilla]] used to gather large quantities of sagebrush seed and grind it to make flour.<ref name="Clarke-1978-p134" /><ref>{{Cite book |author=Jaeger, Edmund C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5xxCG3OfLO8C&pg=PA302 |title=Desert Wild Flowers |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1940 |isbn=9780804703659 |page=302 |author-link=Edmund Jaeger}}</ref> The main modern use is as firewood, with the wood's oils being particularly flammable.<ref name="Knopf" />

=== Medicinal ===
The plant's active medicinal constituents include camphor, terpenoids, and [[tannin]]s.<ref name="shakhnoza" />[[Image:Young sagebrush.JPG|thumb|A young sagebrush grown as [[bonsai]], showing the typical leaf configuration]]

It is used as a [[herbal medicine]] by Native Americans throughout the Intermountain West of North America, most notably as a [[Smudge stick|smudging]] herb. It is also used for preventing infection in wounds, stopping internal bleeding, and treating [[headache]]s and colds.

The [[Navajo people|Navajo]] use the vapors of sagebrush as a treatment for headache.<ref name="Tilford">''Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West'', Gregory L. Tilford, {{ISBN|0878423591}} {{page needed|date=July 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Kay, Margarita|title=Healing with Plants|publisher=University of Arizona Press|year=1996|isbn=9780186516465|pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780186516465/page/106 106]–107|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780186516465|url-access=registration}}</ref> The [[Okanagan people|Okanagan]] and [[Colville people|Colville]] people used sagebrush to smoke hides.<ref>{{cite book|author=Pennacchio, Marcelo|title=Uses and Abuses of Plant-Derived Smoke: Its Ethnobotany As Hallucinogen, Perfume, Incense, and Medicine|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2010|isbn=9780195370010|page=48|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pr9fgQIr5LkC&pg=PA48|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

Among the [[Zuni people]], an infusion of the leaves is used externally for body aches. The infusion is also taken as a cold medicine. It is also placed in shoes to treat [[athlete's foot]], fissures between toes, and as a foot deodorant.<ref>Camazine, Scott and Robert A. Bye 1980 A Study Of The Medical Ethnobotany Of The Zuni Indians of New Mexico" ''Journal of Ethnopharmacology'' 2:365–88 (p. 374)</ref>
